issues.explanation: The Threat items describe a chronic interpersonal/home-intrusion danger template (monitoring for someone entering the home, planning escape routes, feeling unsafe specifically at night), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. These items imply fear of human attack rather than disaster-related threat.

Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure could occur after a disaster, but in combination with the highly interpersonal Threat items it reinforces a different trauma narrative than natural disaster. The Memory items are disaster-compatible, but the Threat cluster is not clinically coherent with that trauma context.

The threat items are centered on anticipating intentional human intrusion or attack (planning escape routes, listening for someone entering the home), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster. Heightened alertness to loud sounds could fit disaster trauma, but these two more specific threat beliefs imply a different trauma context.

The appraisal 'The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down' is possible after a disaster, but in this profile it pulls toward a betrayal/response-failure formulation that is not supported elsewhere by the selected threat or memory items. Combined with the intrusion-focused threat items, it weakens coherence with a natural-disaster trauma profile.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat item about listening for someone entering the home implies an interpersonal/intrusion danger theme that is hard to reconcile with a primary trauma type of natural disaster. For a natural-disaster profile, loud sounds and generalized hypervigilance are plausible, but specifically monitoring for a person entering the home suggests a different trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: The appraisal that institutions failed to protect him is possible after a disaster, but in combination with the home-intrusion threat cue it contributes to a mixed interpersonal-threat profile rather than a coherent natural-disaster formulation. The rest of the profile centers on terror, overwhelm, and disorganized memory, so this item is questionable mainly because it pulls toward a different trauma narrative when paired with the flagged threat item.

vignette: Mark is a 45-year-old widowed European man with a long career as a military medic. His life took an unexpected turn when he was caught in the middle of a catastrophic hurricane while serving abroad. The event was a harrowing experience that left him on high alert even now, months later. He hears unexpected or loud sounds and immediately feels his body tense up, ready to flee or fight at a moment's notice. This hypervigilance has made it nearly impossible for him to relax even in the safety of his own home. Since the disaster, Mark’s memories of that day have been vivid yet fragmented. He remembers flashes of chaos and destruction but struggles to put the events in order. When these memories surface, they bring back the same overwhelming sense of terror he felt during the hurricane itself. The intensity of the emotions forces him to stop what he is doing, often leading to a momentary shutdown that disrupts his daily activities. Mark has come to believe that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore, and he finds it difficult to recognize himself within these experiences. His beliefs about how the world operates have been shattered, leaving him feeling disoriented and uncertain. The hurricane was more than just an environmental event; it challenged everything he thought he knew about safety and control. The memory of that day is so potent because every unexpected sound—a sudden noise outside his window or a loud crackling on the radio—triggers these intense recollections. He is constantly scanning his environment for signs of danger, which feeds into his feeling that he can’t relax even in safe settings. This hypervigilance has made him acutely aware of how fragile and unpredictable life can be. Mark’s sense of meaninglessness deepens when he tries to recall the event. The memories are not just painful; they are also confusing because he cannot sequence them properly, leaving him feeling lost and disoriented. He fears that if he continues to struggle with these memories, his sense of self will erode even further. Each time a memory surfaces, it reinforces his negative appraisals about the world and himself. This vicious cycle has taken a toll on Mark’s daily life. His job as a military medic is particularly challenging because being constantly alert can interfere with his ability to focus and respond effectively in emergencies. He often finds himself overwhelmed by the need to be vigilant, which detracts from his usual calm demeanor and competence at work. Mark’s relationships have also suffered. He has become more distant and less communicative with friends and family who do not fully understand what he is going through. The constant fear and hypervigilance make it hard for him to open up and engage in the ways he once did. What finally brought Mark to seek help was a sense that he could no longer function at his best, both personally and professionally. He is most afraid of losing himself completely but hopes that with support, he can regain some control over his life and find meaning again. His journey towards healing involves acknowledging these fears and working through the memories that continue to haunt him. Mark’s story is one of a man struggling to reconcile the overwhelming chaos of that day with the order he once believed in. Each sound triggers a cycle of hypervigilance, fragmented memories, and deepening negative appraisals. His search for stability and meaning is at the heart of his current struggle, but it also holds the potential for growth and recovery.
